t.1.6.2: A great chariot-warrior among the Ikṣvākus, a performer of sacrifices, devoted to dharma and self-controlled, he was a royal sage almost equal to the great sages, renowned throughout the three worlds.
t.1.6.1: In that city of Ayodhyā lived one who knew the Vedas and drew all things together, a far-sighted man of great splendor, beloved by the people of the city and of the countryside.
t.1.6.3: Mighty, with his enemies slain, rich in friends and master of his senses, he was, by his wealth and by his other stores, the equal of Śakra and Vaiśravaṇa.
t.1.6.4: Just as the mighty and radiant Manu was the protector of the world, so King Daśaratha, dwelling there, protected the world.
t.1.6.5: That city was protected by him, true to his word and devoted to the three aims of life, as Amarāvatī is protected by Indra, the foremost of the gods.
t.1.6.6: In that excellent city the men, gladdened by the righteous-souled one, were deeply learned, content each with his own wealth, free from greed, and speakers of truth.
t.1.6.7: In that finest of cities there was no householder with only a meagre store, none whose aims were unfulfilled, and none who lacked cattle, horses, wealth and grain.
t.1.6.8: Nowhere in Ayodhyā could one see a man who was lustful, miserly, or cruel, nor one who was unlearned, nor an unbeliever.
t.1.6.9: All the men and women were righteous in disposition and well self-controlled, joyful in their good character and conduct, and spotless like the great sages.
t.1.6.10: There is no one there without earrings, without a diadem, or without a garland, no one of meagre enjoyments, no one unbathed, no one whose limbs are unanointed, and no one without fragrance.
t.1.6.11: No one was to be seen there who ate poor food or who did not give charity, no one who did not wear armlets and gold necklaces, no one without ornaments on his hands, and no one lacking self-control.
t.1.6.12: In Ayodhyā there was no brahmin who had not established the sacred fires, none who did not offer sacrifices, and none who did not give gifts by the thousands; nor was there anyone born of a mixing of castes.
t.1.6.13: The brāhmaṇas, who had conquered their senses, were ever devoted to their own duties; they were given to charity and study, and restrained in accepting gifts.
t.1.6.14: At that time there was no one who was an unbeliever, none who was a liar, and none who was lacking in learning; no one was envious, none was incapable, and none was ignorant.
t.1.6.15: In Ayodhyā no one could be seen who was wretched, distracted in mind, or distressed; no man or woman was to be seen who lacked prosperity or was without beauty, nor anyone who lacked devotion to the king.
t.1.6.16: Among the varṇas, from the foremost to the fourth, all men honored the gods and their guests, were long-lived, and took refuge in dharma and truth.
t.1.6.17: The Kṣatriyas held the Brahmins at their head, and the Vaiśyas were devoted followers of the Kṣatriyas; the Śūdras, intent upon their own duty, served the three other classes.
t.1.6.18: That city was well protected by that lord of the Ikṣvākus, just as it had been of old by the wise Manu, lord of men.
t.1.6.19: Of warriors like fire, skilful and unable to bear insult, complete and accomplished in their learning, like lions dwelling in caves.
t.1.6.21: It was filled with elephants born in the Vindhya mountains and in the Himālaya as well, intoxicated and in rut, exceedingly mighty, resembling mountains.
t.1.6.20: The city was filled with the finest horses, born in the land of Kāmboja, and with Vāhlīka steeds, and with those bred in Vanāyu and those born by the rivers, all resembling the horses of Indra.
t.1.6.22: That city was filled with elephants descended from Añjana and from Vāmana, of the Bhadramandra, Bhadramṛga and Mṛgamandra breeds.
t.1.6.23: Ever filled with mountain-like elephants that were always in rut, that city, true to its name, shone forth across two yojanas and more.
t.1.6.24: That king, equal to Śakra, ruled the city of Ayodhyā, true to its name, auspicious, with firm gateways and bars, adorned with wondrous houses and crowded with thousands of people.
